items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “where incoming solar radiation absorbed exceeds outgoing long-wave radiation, as between about 35°N and 35°S”.
items.answer: Radiation surplus
items.markingKey: Radiation surplus: where incoming solar radiation absorbed exceeds outgoing long-wave radiation, as between about 35°N and 35°S. [1]

items.stem: Explain why there is a radiation surplus at low latitudes and a deficit at high latitudes.
items.answer: High sun angles at low latitudes concentrate insolation and rays pass through less atmosphere; at high latitudes low angles spread energy over large areas, more is reflected (snow and ice albedo) and absorbed by the thicker atmosphere path.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Explain how ocean currents transfer heat polewards.
items.answer: Warm currents such as the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio carry warm water from the tropics to higher latitudes, releasing heat to the air; cold currents return cold water towards the equator.
items.markingKey: 1 mark warm; 1 mark cold; 1 mark example [3]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the atmosphere is more important than the oceans in transferring heat from the equator to the poles?
items.answer: For: Winds in the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and mid-latitude depressions carry sensible and latent heat; the atmosphere carries most of the transfer, especially in middle latitudes. Against: Ocean currents carry much of the heat at low latitudes and warm western Europe through the North Atlantic Drift; the thermohaline circulation moves heat over long timescales. Conclusion: The atmosphere carries most heat overall, but oceans dominate at low latitudes and have major regional effects.

items.stem: A student writes: “Without heat transfer, the tropics would keep getting hotter and the poles colder.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Explain the role of latent heat in the global transfer of energy.
items.answer: Evaporation in the tropics stores energy in water vapour, which is carried polewards by winds; when it condenses at higher latitudes the latent heat is released, warming the atmosphere.

items.stem: Explain the operation of the Hadley cell.
items.answer: Intense heating at the equator causes air to rise (low pressure, ITCZ); it spreads polewards at high altitude, cools and sinks at about 30° (subtropical high); surface trade winds return air to the equator.

items.stem: Explain why winds do not blow directly from high to low pressure.
items.answer: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern; friction near the surface also alters direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark Coriolis; 1 mark direction; 1 mark friction [3]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the tri-cellular model fully explains global patterns of pressure and winds?
items.answer: For: It explains the equatorial low, subtropical highs, mid-latitude westerlies, sub-polar lows and polar highs, and the trade winds. Against: Real patterns are disrupted by continents and oceans (seasonal Asian high and low), relief, ocean currents, jet streams and Rossby waves, monsoons and the seasonal shift of belts with the overhead sun. Conclusion: The model explains the broad zonal pattern well but not regional and seasonal variations.

items.answer: Not correct. They blow from the north-east and south-east towards the equator, i.e. from east to west.

items.stem: Explain how ocean currents influence the climate of coastal areas.
items.answer: Warm currents raise temperatures and humidity (North Atlantic Drift keeps Norway’s ports ice-free); cold currents cool coasts, stabilise air and reduce rainfall, contributing to deserts (Atacama, Namib) and advection fog.
items.markingKey: 1 mark warm; 1 mark cold; 1 mark example [3]

items.stem: On a synoptic chart for a region in the Northern Hemisphere, the centre of a high-pressure system is 1033 hPa and the centre of a low-pressure system 600 km to the north is 1006 hPa. Explain why surface winds cross isobars at an angle while upper winds blow parallel to them.
items.answer: Surface friction reduces wind speed and so the Coriolis effect, so the pressure gradient force pulls the wind across isobars towards low pressure; aloft there is no friction (geostrophic balance).

items.stem: Explain why the ITCZ moves north and south during the year.
items.answer: It follows the zone of maximum heating, the overhead sun, which migrates between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn; its movement is greater over land, which heats and cools faster than the sea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark overhead sun; 1 mark land v sea [2]

items.stem: Explain the causes of the winter (north-east) monsoon in South Asia.
items.answer: The land cools, forming high pressure over central Asia; the ITCZ moves south; dry, cool winds blow out from the land, giving a dry season (except south-east India and Sri Lanka, which receive rain from winds crossing the Bay of Bengal).

To what extent do you agree that the movement of the ITCZ is the only cause of seasonal rainfall in tropical areas?
items.answer: For: The ITCZ brings convectional rain as it follows the overhead sun, giving wet seasons in savanna and monsoon lands. Indicative content: Winds in the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and mid-latitude depressions carry sensible and latent heat; the atmosphere carries most of the transfer, especially in middle latitudes. Ocean currents carry much of the heat at low latitudes and warm western Europe through the North Atlantic Drift; the thermohaline circulation moves heat over long timescales. Judgement: The atmosphere carries most heat overall, but oceans dominate at low latitudes and have major regional effects.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The ITCZ is an area of low pressure with rising air and heavy rain.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Converging trade winds and intense heating produce convection and cumulonimbus clouds.

items.stem: Explain why the tri-cellular model is a simplification.
items.answer: Land and sea heating differences, seasonal migration of pressure belts, mountain barriers, jet streams and Rossby waves, and monsoons all disrupt the idealised pattern.

items.stem: Using the tri-cellular model, state the expected pressure belt or wind belt and the prevailing surface wind for each location: A 57°N; B 1°N; C 64°N. Explain one of your answers.
items.answer: A: mid-latitude westerlies between the subtropical high and sub-polar low; south-westerly winds. B: equatorial low pressure (ITCZ, doldrums); light, variable winds with rising air. C: polar easterlies between the polar high and sub-polar low; north-easterly winds. Explanation: e.g. winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected by the Coriolis effect (right in the north, left in the south).

items.stem: On a synoptic chart for a region in the Northern Hemisphere, the centre of a high-pressure system is 1033 hPa and the centre of a low-pressure system 500 km to the north is 1003 hPa. (a) State the general direction from which the surface wind blows between the two systems, and explain why. (b) Explain why surface winds cross isobars at an angle while upper winds blow parallel to them.
items.answer: (a) Air moves from high pressure (south) towards low pressure (north) but is deflected by the Coriolis effect (right), so the wind blows from the south-west (a south-westerly wind). (b) Surface friction reduces wind speed and so the Coriolis effect, so the pressure gradient force pulls the wind across isobars towards low pressure; aloft there is no friction (geostrophic balance).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark direction; 1 mark pressure gradient; 1 mark Coriolis [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)”?
options: The part of the year when the ITCZ lies overhead and convectional rain falls.
The zone of low pressure where the trade winds converge near the equator, associated with rising air and heavy rain.
The line of highest surface temperature around the globe, which moves north and south with the overhead sun.
A seasonal reversal of wind direction that brings a distinct wet season and dry season.
items.answer: The zone of low pressure where the trade winds converge near the equator, associated with rising air and heavy rain.
items.markingKey: Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ): the zone of low pressure where the trade winds converge near the equator, associated with rising air and heavy rain. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A delayed monsoon can cause economic problems in India.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Farm output, rural incomes and food prices depend on timely monsoon rain.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Places further from the equator in the tropics tend to have shorter wet seasons.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “The ITCZ stays over the equator all year.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. The ITCZ spends less time over them, so the wet season is shorter and rainfall totals lower. (b) Not correct. It migrates seasonally, following the overhead sun, especially far over continents.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Ocean currents only move heat from west to east.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “The poles receive no solar radiation at all.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. They move heat polewards (e.g. Gulf Stream) and cold water equatorwards (e.g. Canary, Benguela). (b) Not correct. They receive radiation in summer, including 24-hour daylight, but at very low angles.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “The Coriolis effect is strongest at the equator.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the operation of the Hadley cell.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. It is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles. (b) Intense heating at the equator causes air to rise (low pressure, ITCZ); it spreads polewards at high altitude, cools and sinks at about 30° (subtropical high); surface trade winds return air to the equator.

The part of the year when the ITCZ lies overhead and convectional rain falls.
The moist summer wind that blows onto South Asia from the Indian Ocean between June and September.
A seasonal reversal of wind direction that brings a distinct wet season and dry season.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Places further from the equator in the tropics tend to have shorter wet seasons.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the causes of the winter (north-east) monsoon in South Asia.
items.answer: (a) Correct. The ITCZ spends less time over them, so the wet season is shorter and rainfall totals lower. (b) The land cools, forming high pressure over central Asia; the ITCZ moves south; dry, cool winds blow out from the land, giving a dry season (except south-east India and Sri Lanka, which receive rain from winds crossing the Bay of Bengal).
